analysis.one_liner: Lets independent musicians jointly negotiate and withhold their music from big streaming and AI companies without antitrust liability.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would let independent musicians bargain collectively with streaming and AI companies, has sat in the House Judiciary Committee since its May 2026 introduction, with three cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change antitrust law so that small, independent musicians — those who own their own recordings and make less than $1 million a year from them — could band together to negotiate licensing terms with big streaming services and generative AI companies, including the right to collectively withhold their music. Under current law, that kind of coordinated action by copyright owners can be treated as illegal price-fixing. The bill was introduced in May 2026 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent musicians, producers, mixers, and sound engineers who own their own recordings and earn under $1 million a year from them. The bill would let them join together to negotiate licensing terms — and to jointly refuse to license their music at all — to big streaming platforms and to companies making generative AI, without fear of being sued under antitrust laws. Today, antitrust law treats such joint action as potentially illegal price-fixing, which leaves each small artist to negotiate alone against companies vastly larger than they are.

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives small musicians, producers, and sound engineers who own their recordings a legal safe harbor to negotiate licensing terms as a group with dominant streaming platforms and generative AI companies, ending their current isolation in one-on-one negotiations.

It lets them collectively refuse to license their music to these companies, the same leverage a union gets from the threat of a strike, which the bill's findings say is the only way to counter platforms that otherwise 'simply ignore' artists who reject their terms.

The safe harbor is limited to creators earning under $1 million a year (or qualifying as a small music business) and to platforms with over $100 million in music-distribution revenue, so it targets bargaining power at the largest companies without extending it to large labels or dominant rights holders.

analysis.who_pays: Dominant music streaming platforms and companies building generative AI music tools would bear the cost if the bill passes: they would have to negotiate licensing terms with groups of small artists and could no longer count on being able to use unlicensed music without consequence. Some of those costs would likely show up as higher licensing payments, and possibly higher subscription prices, though the bill only covers platforms with more than $100 million in annual music-distribution revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Streaming platforms and AI music developers

drawbacks.text: Antitrust exemptions are generally disfavored because letting competitors coordinate on prices can raise costs, and the bill itself acknowledges this in its findings; if a critical mass of artists collectively withholds music, platforms could pass higher licensing costs to subscribers as higher prices.

The safe harbor's conditions are loose enough to invite disputes: it requires that negotiations be nondiscriminatory and 'reasonably necessary,' but does not create a mechanism for determining when a collective refusal crosses from bargaining leverage into an unlawful boycott, leaving courts and the FTC to sort it out.

The bill exempts services eligible for statutory licenses under copyright law's section 114(d)(2), so the biggest interactive streaming services operating under those licenses fall outside the definition in some readings, and the practical reach of the bill against the very platforms it names depends on how courts apply that carve-out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: it would hand genuine negotiating leverage to a group of creators who currently have none, using the same logic that lets workers unionize. The costs are contained because the exemption applies only to small rights holders, only against very large platforms and AI companies, and only if negotiations meet nondiscrimination conditions — though, as with any price coordination, some of the cost could land on subscribers, and the bill's carve-outs may blunt its reach. The larger problem is not the design but the fate: a three-cosponsor bill in committee changes nothing until it moves.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee in May 2026 and has not moved since; Congress is still in session, so it is sitting in committee awaiting action that has not come.

narrative.text: Rep. Deborah Ross introduced the Protect Working Musicians Act of 2026 on May 21, 2026, with Reps. Steve Cohen and Lloyd Doggett as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee, the committee that handles copyright and antitrust law, and no further action has been taken on it.
The bill has three cosponsors, all House Democrats, and neither chamber has voted on it.

The bill would create a safe harbor from antitrust liability allowing individual music creator owners to collectively negotiate with, or collectively refuse to license to, dominant online music distribution platforms and generative AI companies.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the dominant streaming platforms and generative AI developers are better off: they face no new obligation to bargain with small artists and no risk of a coordinated license boycott. Independent musicians have gained nothing, and their records remain exposed to unlicensed use on the same terms as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Streaming platforms and AI developers, untouched so far

for.name: Rep. Deborah Ross
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

sides.party_line_note: Only three House Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill and no votes have occurred, so no partisan split has taken shape; the fight so far is between the sponsors and an inactive committee.

industries.note: Services with more than $100 million in annual music-distribution revenue would face groups of small artists negotiating together and the threat of a coordinated license boycott, which would cut into the leverage they use to set low royalty rates. Their interest in stopping the bill runs against the artists' interest in higher pay.

Companies building or deploying generative AI would lose the ability to deal with small rights holders one by one and could face a collective refusal to license music for training or output. Their interest runs against the artists the bill protects.

The bill is limited to creators who own their own recordings and earn under $1 million a year, and it bars participation by anyone else, so major labels and large labels' corporate structures are excluded from the safe harbor. It does not regulate them directly, but it does not extend them the new negotiating power either.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the House Judiciary Committee with only three cosponsors and no committee action since its referral. Most bills at this stage, this early in their committee's docket and with this little support, never receive a markup or floor vote; this one would need a committee chairman to schedule it and far more bipartisan support to move.
